steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper on zero-shot relation triplet extraction using prompts and semantic knowledge. Motivate zero-shot extraction, describe the shortcomings of existing approaches, outline our model, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Relation triplet extraction and the need for zero-shot learning
- Zero-shot RTE task and limitations of existing approaches
- Our model (ZS-SKA): data augmentation
- Knowledge-graph-based prompts with virtual label words
- Prototypical networks and triplet prediction
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- RTE
  - extract pairs of entities and relations from unstructured text
  - supervised (cite) and few-shot (cite) approaches still need labeled data; can't keep up with new classes
  - classes rare or unseen in training -> learn like humans -> zero-shot learning (ZSL)
  - same ZSL definition as prior work (cite)
- Zero-shot RTE
  - extract triplets with relations absent at training; Figure 1 example
  - train and test relation sets disjoint; train on seen, extract unseen
  - limitation 1: question answering (cite) or GPT-2 synthetic data (cite); assume extra model is excellent and its outputs correct
  - limitation 2: text entailment (cite); only binary label for whether entities match a description
  - limitation 3: auxiliary info (class names/descriptions), lose connections between seen and unseen relations (cite)
  - mostly zero-shot relation classification (ZSRC): predicts relations, not <head entity, relation, tail entity> triplets; assumes two name entities given -> not realistic
- ZS-SKA: augmentation
  - word-level sentence translation: augmented instances with unseen relations from seen ones
  - generation rule in Sec. 3.2.1; trained only on seen-class labels + augmented data
- Prompts
  - inspired by prompt-tuning on pre-trained language models (cite)
  - knowledge-graph prompts to infer unseen relations from seen patterns
  - semantic knowledge: relation descriptions, super-class of relations and name entities, general knowledge graph
  - automatically search label words per label via knowledge graph; weights in Sec. 3.2.2
  - distance to true label to denoise; virtual label words by weighted averaging
- Prototypes
  - prototypical networks (cite); prototype = mean vector of embedded + augmented sentences with prompts
  - Euclidean distance query vs prototypes; distance threshold from validation set -> number of triplets
  - name entity extractor; sorted entity types vs super-class in prompt -> final triplets
- Contributions
  - ZS-SKA for unseen-relation triplets; multiple granularities; no other large models
  - word-level sentence translation rule for augmentation; training sets for unseen relations
  - external-knowledge-graph prompts; weighted virtual label words for the mask
  - significantly outperforms SOTA on three public datasets

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Relation triplet extraction (RTE) aims to extract both the pairs of entities and the relations from unstructured text. But existing approaches, whether based on supervised learning or few-shot learning, still need labeled data. They can not keep up with a dynamic and open environment where new classes appear. In the real world, the classes of instances are sometimes rare or never seen in the training data. So we want to learn a model in a way that is similar to how humans learn and recognize new concepts. This task is called zero-shot learning (ZSL). We use the same definition of ZSL as previous work for our experiments.

Zero-shot RTE aims to extract relation triplets in a sentence that are absent from the learning stage. Figure 1 shows an example of zero-shot RTE. The relation sets in the training and testing stages are disjoint. The model is only trained on the seen relations in the training stage, and in the testing stage it extracts triplets with unseen relations. Existing approaches to zero-shot relation extraction still have limitations. First, some models do zero-shot relation extraction by question answering or use GPT-2 to help generate synthetic data. These models strongly assume that an excellent additional deep learning model has been learned and that all the values extracted from it are correct. Second, some studies formulate relation extraction as a text entailment task. They only predict a binary label saying whether the name entities in the sentence can be described by a given description. Third, some SOTA models use auxiliary information for zero-shot tasks. They focus on class names/descriptions and lose the connection or relationships between seen and unseen relations. Also, these works mainly focus on zero-shot relation classification (ZSRC), which only predicts unseen relations and not triplets in the format of <head entity, relation, tail entity>. ZSRC strongly assumes that two name entities are available for training, but it is not realistic that the name entities are already given.

To address these challenges we propose a prompt-based model with semantic knowledge augmentation (ZS-SKA) for zero-shot RTE. First we do data augmentation with a word-level sentence translation, which generates augmented instances with unseen relations from training instances with seen relations. We follow a new generation rule, introduced in Sec. 3.2.1, to generate high-quality augmented instances for training in zero-shot settings. Note that ZS-SKA is trained only on labeled data from seen classes and on augmented data generated from seen classes.

Prompts
- inspired by prompt-tuning on pre-trained language models
- knowledge-graph prompts: relation descriptions, super-class of relations and name entities, general knowledge graph
- search appropriate label words per label; weights in Sec. 3.2.2; denoise by distance to true label
- virtual label words by weighted averaging

Prototypes and triplets
- prototypical networks; prototype = mean of embedded + augmented sentences with prompts
- Euclidean distance; threshold from validation set decides number of triplets
- name entity extractor; entity types vs super-class in prompt

Contributions
- ZS-SKA; different granularities; no other large models
- word-level sentence translation rule for augmentation
- knowledge-graph prompts with weighted virtual label words
- outperforms SOTA on three public datasets

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Relation triplet extraction (RTE) aims to extract both the pairs of entities and the relations from unstructured text. But existing approaches, whether based on supervised learning or few-shot learning, still need labeled data. They can not keep up with a dynamic and open environment where new classes appear. In the real world, the classes of instances are sometimes rare or never seen in the training data. So we want to learn a model in a way that is similar to how humans learn and recognize new concepts. This task is called zero-shot learning (ZSL). We use the same definition of ZSL as previous work for our experiments.

Zero-shot RTE aims to extract relation triplets in a sentence that are absent from the learning stage. Figure 1 shows an example of zero-shot RTE. The relation sets in the training and testing stages are disjoint. The model is only trained on the seen relations in the training stage, and in the testing stage it extracts triplets with unseen relations. Existing approaches to zero-shot relation extraction still have limitations. First, some models do zero-shot relation extraction by question answering or use GPT-2 to help generate synthetic data. These models strongly assume that an excellent additional deep learning model has been learned and that all the values extracted from it are correct. Second, some studies formulate relation extraction as a text entailment task. They only predict a binary label saying whether the name entities in the sentence can be described by a given description. Third, some SOTA models use auxiliary information for zero-shot tasks. They focus on class names/descriptions and lose the connection or relationships between seen and unseen relations. Also, these works mainly focus on zero-shot relation classification (ZSRC), which only predicts unseen relations and not triplets in the format of <head entity, relation, tail entity>. ZSRC strongly assumes that two name entities are available for training, but it is not realistic that the name entities are already given.

To address these challenges we propose a prompt-based model with semantic knowledge augmentation (ZS-SKA) for zero-shot RTE. First we do data augmentation with a word-level sentence translation, which generates augmented instances with unseen relations from training instances with seen relations. We follow a new generation rule, introduced in Sec. 3.2.1, to generate high-quality augmented instances for training in zero-shot settings. Note that ZS-SKA is trained only on labeled data from seen classes and on augmented data generated from seen classes.

Second, inspired by prompt-tuning on pre-trained language models, we design prompts based on the knowledge graph, which integrate semantic knowledge so that the features of unseen relations can be inferred using patterns learned from seen relations. In the prompt design we consider semantic knowledge information, including relation descriptions, the super-class of relations and name entities, and a general knowledge graph, to learn the unseen relations effectively. We do not use the real label word directly in the prompt template. Instead we automatically search a set of appropriate label words for each label based on the knowledge graph. The weight of each appropriate label word is calculated from its semantic knowledge information in Sec. 3.2.2. We calculate the distance between each appropriate label and the true label itself to help denoise the set of appropriate label words. Then we build virtual label words in the prompt by weighted averaging of all the appropriate label word candidates.

Finally we use prototypical networks to compute a prototype for each relation. Each prototype is the mean vector of the embedded and augmented sentences with prompts that belong to one relation. We calculate the Euclidean distance between the query sentence embeddings and the prototypes to predict relations. A distance threshold found on the validation set decides the number of relation triplets. For name entity predictions we use a name entity extractor to recognize the different types of entities. Then the sorted entity types are compared with the super-class of name entities in the prompt to decide the final relation triplets. Our contributions are:

- We propose a prompt-based model with semantic knowledge augmentation (ZS-SKA) that extracts triplets with unseen relations in the zero-shot setting. Unlike some previous works, ZS-SKA uses semantic information from different granularities and does not depend on other large models with additional training.

- We present a new word-level sentence translation rule that generates augmented instances with unseen relations from instances with seen relations. The augmented sentences are then used as training sets for the unseen relations.

- We propose prompts for training based on an external knowledge graph, which integrate semantic knowledge information learned from seen relations. We build weighted virtual label words for the mask in the prompt template instead of using the actual label sets.

- We show that ZS-SKA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods for relation extraction with unseen relations in the ZSL setting on three public datasets.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Relation triplet extraction (RTE) aims to extract both the pairs of entities and the relations from unstructured text. However, existing approaches based on supervised learning [1,2,3,4,5,6] or few-shot learning [7,8,9,10,11,12] still require labeled data, and they can not keep up with a dynamic and open environment where new classes emerge. In real-world settings, the classes of instances are sometimes rare or never seen in the training data. We therefore aim to learn a model in a way similar to how humans learn and recognize new concepts, a task referred to as zero-shot learning (ZSL). We follow the same definition of ZSL as in [13,14] to conduct experiments.

Zero-shot RTE aims to extract relation triplets in a sentence that are absent from the learning stage. Figure 1 shows an example of zero-shot RTE. The relation sets at the training and testing stages are disjoint: the model is trained only on the seen relations in the training stage and extracts triplets with unseen relations in the testing stage. Existing approaches to zero-shot relation extraction still have limitations. First, some models perform zero-shot relation extraction by question answering [15] or by using GPT-2 to help generate synthetic data [13]. These models strongly assume that an excellent additional deep learning model has been learned and that all values extracted from it are correct. Second, some existing studies formulate relation extraction as a text entailment task [16], predicting only a binary label that indicates whether the name entities in the given sentence can be described by a given description. Third, some SOTA models leverage auxiliary information to tackle zero-shot tasks. Focusing on class names/descriptions, they lose the connection or relationships between seen and unseen relations [17,14,18]. Besides, these works mainly focus on zero-shot relation classification (ZSRC), which only predicts unseen relations rather than triplets in the format of <head entity, relation, tail entity>. ZSRC strongly assumes that two name entities are available for training, yet it is not realistic that name entities are already provided.

To address these challenges, we propose a prompt-based model with semantic knowledge augmentation (ZS-SKA) to perform zero-shot RTE. We first implement data augmentation through a word-level sentence translation that generates augmented instances with unseen relations from training instances with seen relations. Following a new generation rule introduced in Sec. 3.2.1, we generate high-quality augmented instances for training in zero-shot settings. Note that ZS-SKA is trained only on labeled data from seen classes and on augmented data generated from seen classes.

Secondly, inspired by prompt-tuning on pre-trained language models [19,20], we design prompts based on the knowledge graph that integrate semantic knowledge, so as to infer the features of unseen relations using patterns learned from seen relations. For the prompt design, we consider semantic knowledge information, including relation descriptions, the super-class of relations and name entities, and a general knowledge graph, to learn the unseen relations effectively. Instead of using the real label word directly in the prompt template, we automatically search a set of appropriate label words for each label based on the knowledge graph. The weight of each appropriate label word is calculated from its semantic knowledge information in Sec. 3.2.2. We calculate the distance between each appropriate label and the true label itself to help denoise the set of appropriate label words. We then construct virtual label words in the prompt by weighted averaging of all appropriate label word candidates.

Finally, we apply prototypical networks [21] to compute a prototype representing each relation, where each prototype is the mean vector of the embedded and augmented sentences with prompts belonging to one relation. The Euclidean distance between query sentence embeddings and prototypes is calculated to predict relations, and a distance threshold explored on the validation set determines the number of relation triplets. For name entity predictions, we use a name entity extractor to recognize different types of entities; the sorted entity types are then compared with the super-class of name entities in the prompt to determine the final relation triplets. Our contributions are:

- We propose a prompt-based model with semantic knowledge augmentation (ZS-SKA) to extract triplets with unseen relations under the zero-shot setting. Unlike some previous works, ZS-SKA considers semantic information from different granularities and does not rely on other large models with additional training.

- We present a new word-level sentence translation rule to generate augmented instances with unseen relations from instances with seen relations. The augmented sentences are then used as the training sets for unseen relations.

- We propose prompts for training based on an external knowledge graph to integrate semantic knowledge information learned from seen relations, and construct weighted virtual label words for the mask in the prompt template instead of using the actual label sets.

- We demonstrate that ZS-SKA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods for relation extraction with unseen relations under the ZSL setting on three public datasets.
